: **The running machine's card**: The fifteen parameters of the warehouse mobile manipulator that later calculations use most. A derived value built on illustrative inputs is illustrative evidence. Values print from the MLSysIM registry when the book is built. {#tbl-01-machine-card tbl-colwidths="[24,12,12,52]"}

With these parameters fixed, every later design problem on this platform starts from the same physical foundation. It asks which margin a commanded action approaches and whether the machine can execute an assured protective response before that margin is exhausted. The first margin to price is stopping clearance, and four rows of the card, the drive limit, the credible deceleration, the clear distance, and the pre-brake delay, are enough to price it.

### Delay consumes stopping clearance {#sec-boundary-kinematic-roofline}

A moving vehicle requires dedicated stopping clearance across two distinct phases: distance traveled before braking forces engage, and distance traversed while mechanical braking brings momentum to zero. Assuming steady initial velocity $\SpeedAtDetection$, uniform deceleration $\CredibleBrakingDeceleration$ once brakes engage, and a stationary obstacle, the elementary stopping distance satisfies the kinematic budget:
$$\StoppingDistance = \underbrace{\SpeedAtDetection \PrebrakeDelay}_{\text{travel during response delay}} + \underbrace{\frac{\SpeedAtDetection^2}{2 \CredibleBrakingDeceleration}}_{\text{mechanical dissipation}} \le \ClearDistance$$ {#eq-boundary-stopping-budget}
Here $\SpeedAtDetection$ denotes initial forward speed, $\PrebrakeDelay$ represents total pre-brake response latency, $\CredibleBrakingDeceleration$ is the sustained braking deceleration, and $\ClearDistance$ is the usable line-of-sight clearance. The pre-brake delay $\PrebrakeDelay$ spans the time from when an obstacle first appears in a sensor exposure to the physical onset of retarding force. Specifically, it sums the age of the sensor observation upon handoff, the unexpired lease duration of any currently executing motion chunk (the lease is the longest an admitted chunk may drive before the permission path must act again), one discrete permission-path evaluation tick (the period at which the permission path re-checks the motion it has admitted), one bus communication cycle (the time to carry a command to the motor drives), and mechanical brake onset latency.

The lease belongs in the worst case even though the permission path re-checks every tick, because of what that check can see. Each tick tests the admitted chunk against limits the permission path already holds (the chunk's freshness, its lease, and the kinematic bounds, measured against the wheel and joint encoders); the permission path has no camera pipeline of its own. On the detection path this budget models, evidence that a worker has stepped out therefore reaches the brakes only through the learned perception path and a replacement proposal. If the proposer stalls or fails to answer the worker, the most recently admitted chunk keeps driving until its lease expires, and only then does the permission path command the stop. The term deliberately excludes one interval, the dispatch-to-admission interval (the time while the learned policy computes a replacement proposal and the permission path admits it). Its length depends on where the proposer and the permission path run and how they communicate, decisions this chapter has not yet made, so @sec-placement-dispatch-admission allocates it and the finished budget pays for it from the spare this elementary budget leaves.

The budget has two terms that grow differently with speed: travel during the delay grows linearly ($\SpeedAtDetection \PrebrakeDelay$), and travel while shedding kinetic energy grows with the square of speed ($\SpeedAtDetection^2 / (2 \CredibleBrakingDeceleration)$). Equating them gives the crossover speed $\StoppingCrossoverSpeed = 2 \CredibleBrakingDeceleration \PrebrakeDelay$. Below $\StoppingCrossoverSpeed$, delay travel is the larger term; above it, braking travel dominates. Shortening sensing, computation, and signaling reduces the delay term, while lowering speed reduces both terms: halving speed halves the delay travel and quarters the braking travel. Which change saves more clearance depends on the reductions available, not on term dominance alone. Solving @eq-boundary-stopping-budget for $\SpeedAtDetection$ gives the fastest speed whose stop fits inside a verified clear distance, a ceiling @sec-body-dynamic-velocity-ceilings derives with the allowances this elementary form omits.

```{python}
#| label: boundary-stopping-budget
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ THE RUNNING MACHINE'S ELEMENTARY STOPPING BUDGET (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @nbk-boundary-stopping-budget in @sec-boundary-kinematic-roofline,
# │          and the takeaways.
# │ Goal:    Close the stopping inequality against the card's clear distance,
# │          open the pre-brake delay into its registry terms, and show the
# │          crossover speed and a half-speed what-if.
# │ Show:    133.6 ms = 51.6 + 60 + 1 + 1 + 20 ms; 200.4 + 562.5 = 762.9 mm
# │          inside 1.10 m (337.1 mm spare); v* = 0.53 m/s; backbone 22 ms is
# │          33 mm; at 0.75 m/s the stop is 240.8 mm. Guard: the finished
# │          budget of @sec-enforcement-composite-budget exceeds D_clear at the
# │          drive limit, which the prose states without printing it.
# │ How:     RM/AISLE fields from the warehouse mobile manipulator in mlsysim;
# │          the guard reuses calc_c2_stop_suffix and calc_scurve_stop_distance
# │          exactly as @sec-enforcement-composite-budget does. No value is retyped.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.physics.robotics import calc_c2_stop_suffix, calc_scurve_stop_distance
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_length, fmt_latency, fmt_velocity, fmt_acceleration, fmt_percent, fmt_multiple, fmt_display_math, check

RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
AISLE = Embodied.Scenario.WarehouseAisle

class StoppingBudget:
    """Elementary stopping budget of the loaded base at its drive limit (illustrative inputs)."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    v = RM.base.max_velocity  # category: illustrative (drive limit)
    v_aisle = AISLE.v_aisle  # category: chosen (aisle speed on the card)
    a_brake = AISLE.a_brake  # category: illustrative (credible deceleration, loaded, dry floor)
    d_clear = AISLE.d_clear  # category: illustrative (rack-end clear distance)
    t_age = AISLE.perception_age  # category: derived (mid-exposure to proposer dispatch)
    t_backbone = AISLE.t_backbone  # category: illustrative (perception backbone, inside t_age)
    t_lease = AISLE.t_lease  # category: chosen (chunk lease)
    t_tick = AISLE.t_tick  # category: chosen (one permission tick)
    t_bus = AISLE.t_bus  # category: illustrative (one bus cycle)
    t_onset = AISLE.t_brake_onset  # category: illustrative (brake command to retarding force)
    tau_delay = AISLE.tau_delay  # category: derived (sum of the five terms above)

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    tau_sum = (t_age + t_lease + t_tick + t_bus + t_onset).to(millisecond)
    blind = (v * tau_delay).to(millimeter)
    d_brake = (v**2 / (2 * a_brake)).to(millimeter)
    d_stop = (blind + d_brake).to(millimeter)
    spare = (d_clear - d_stop).to(millimeter)
    blind_share = (blind / d_brake).to("dimensionless").magnitude
    brake_over_blind = (d_brake / blind).to("dimensionless").magnitude
    v_star = (2 * a_brake * tau_delay).to(meter / second)
    d_backbone = (v * t_backbone).to(millimeter)
    d_lease = (v * t_lease).to(millimeter)
    d_per_ms = (v * (1 * millisecond)).to(millimeter)
    v_half = v / 2
    blind_half = (v_half * tau_delay).to(millimeter)
    brake_half = (v_half**2 / (2 * a_brake)).to(millimeter)
    d_stop_half = (blind_half + brake_half).to(millimeter)
    # Guard only: the finished budget of @sec-enforcement-composite-budget at the drive limit
    j_brake = calc_c2_stop_suffix(v, a_brake)["peak_jerk"].to(meter / second**3)
    d_finished = (calc_scurve_stop_distance(v, a_brake, j_brake) + blind + AISLE.delta_loc + AISLE.delta_margin + AISLE.eps_track).to(millimeter)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs(tau_sum.magnitude - tau_delay.to(millisecond).magnitude) < 1e-9, "tau_delay must equal its five registry terms.")
    check(abs(tau_delay.to(millisecond).magnitude - 133.6) < 5e-3, f"Canon tau_delay is 133.6 ms, got {tau_delay}.")
    check(abs(d_stop.magnitude - 762.9) < 5e-3, f"Canon elementary stop is 762.9 mm, got {d_stop}.")
    check(spare.magnitude > 0, "The elementary budget must fit inside D_clear at the drive limit.")
    check(v_star < v, "At the drive limit braking, not delay, must dominate.")
    check(d_finished > d_clear, "Prose says the finished budget exceeds D_clear at the drive limit.")
    check(v_aisle < v, "Prose says the aisle speed sits below the drive limit.")
    # margin_prebrake_delay_composition_bar.svg fig-alt hand-types 29.6, 2, and 20 ms
    check(abs((t_age - t_backbone).to(millisecond).magnitude - 29.6) < 5e-3, "fig-alt: rest of observation age is 29.6 ms.")
    check(abs((t_tick + t_bus).to(millisecond).magnitude - 2.0) < 1e-9, "fig-alt: tick plus bus is 2 ms.")
    check(abs(t_onset.to(millisecond).magnitude - 20.0) < 1e-9, "fig-alt: brake onset is 20 ms.")
    check(t_lease > t_age, "Margin caption says the lease costs more than the backbone; it is the largest term.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    v_str = fmt_velocity(v, unit=meter / second, precision=1)
    v_aisle_str = fmt_velocity(v_aisle, unit=meter / second, precision=1)
    a_brake_str = fmt_acceleration(a_brake, unit=meter / second**2)
    d_clear_str = fmt_length(d_clear, unit=meter, precision=2)
    tau_delay_str = fmt_latency(tau_delay, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    t_age_str = fmt_latency(t_age, unit=millisecond, precision=1)
    t_backbone_str = fmt_latency(t_backbone, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_lease_str = fmt_latency(t_lease, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_tick_str = fmt_latency(t_tick, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_bus_str = fmt_latency(t_bus, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    t_onset_str = fmt_latency(t_onset, unit=millisecond, precision=0)
    spare_str = fmt_length(spare, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    blind_share_str = fmt_percent(blind_share, precision=1, style="prose")
    brake_over_blind_mult_str = fmt_multiple(brake_over_blind, precision=1)
    d_backbone_str = fmt_length(d_backbone, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    d_lease_str = fmt_length(d_lease, unit=millimeter, precision=0)
    d_per_ms_str = fmt_length(d_per_ms, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    v_half_str = fmt_velocity(v_half, unit=meter / second, precision=2)
    d_stop_half_str = fmt_length(d_stop_half, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    blind_half_str = fmt_length(blind_half, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    brake_half_str = fmt_length(brake_half, unit=millimeter, precision=1)

    _v = fmt(v, unit=meter / second, precision=1)
    _a = fmt(a_brake, unit=meter / second**2, precision=0)
    _tau_s = fmt(tau_delay, unit=second, precision=4)
    _blind = fmt(blind, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    _brake = fmt(d_brake, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    _stop = fmt(d_stop, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    _clear = fmt(d_clear, unit=millimeter, precision=0, commas=False)
    _spare = fmt(spare, unit=millimeter, precision=1)
    _vstar = fmt(v_star, unit=meter / second, precision=2)
    tau_sum_math = fmt_display_math(
        rf"\tau_{{\text{{delay}}}} = {fmt(t_age, unit=millisecond, precision=1)} + {fmt(t_lease, unit=millisecond, precision=0)} + {fmt(t_tick, unit=millisecond, precision=0)} + {fmt(t_bus, unit=millisecond, precision=0)} + {fmt(t_onset, unit=millisecond, precision=0)} = {fmt(tau_delay, unit=millisecond, precision=1)}\ \text{{ms}}"
    )
    blind_math = fmt_display_math(rf"v\,\tau_{{\text{{delay}}}} = {_v}\ \text{{m/s}} \times {_tau_s}\ \text{{s}} = {_blind}\ \text{{mm}}")
    brake_math = fmt_display_math(
        rf"\frac{{v^2}}{{2 a_{{\text{{brake}}}}}} = \frac{{({_v}\ \text{{m/s}})^2}}{{2 \times {_a}\ \text{{m/s}}^2}} = {_brake}\ \text{{mm}}"
    )
    close_math = fmt_display_math(
        rf"d_{{\text{{stop}}}} = {_blind} + {_brake} = {_stop}\ \text{{mm}} \le D_{{\text{{clear}}}} = {_clear}\ \text{{mm}}, \quad D_{{\text{{clear}}}} - d_{{\text{{stop}}}} = {_spare}\ \text{{mm}}"
    )
    vstar_math = fmt_display_math(
        rf"v^{{*}} = 2 a_{{\text{{brake}}}} \tau_{{\text{{delay}}}} = 2 \times {_a}\ \text{{m/s}}^2 \times {_tau_s}\ \text{{s}} \approx {_vstar}\ \text{{m/s}}"
    )
```

Every input to the budget comes from the running machine. Its speed, deceleration, clear distance, and pre-brake delay are rows of the machine card (@tbl-01-machine-card), and the five terms of that delay come from the same MLSysIM registry, so the notebook's givens are the ones every later chapter refines.

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/margin_prebrake_delay_composition_bar.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="One stacked horizontal bar for the 133.6 milliseconds of pre-brake delay, bracketed above. Left to right: the learned model's backbone, 22 milliseconds, in orange; the rest of the observation age, 29.6; the chunk lease, 60 milliseconds, in dark slate and the widest segment; a thin sliver of 2 for the permission tick and bus cycle; and brake onset, 20. All other segments are gray."}

*The learned backbone is `{python} StoppingBudget.t_backbone_str` of the `{python} StoppingBudget.tau_delay_str` delay; the lease costs more.*
:::

::: {#nbk-boundary-stopping-budget .callout-notebook title="Does the base stop inside its clearance?"}

**Problem**: The loaded base cruises toward a rack end at its drive limit, and a worker may step out at the end of the rack. The permission path must stop the base inside the rack-end clear distance on the machine card. Does the elementary stopping budget of @eq-boundary-stopping-budget fit, which term dominates, and how much of the delay belongs to the learned model?

**Variables**:

* Speed $\SpeedAtDetection =$ `{python} StoppingBudget.v_str`, the drive limit (illustrative).
* Credible deceleration $\CredibleBrakingDeceleration =$ `{python} StoppingBudget.a_brake_str`, loaded on a dry floor (illustrative).
* Clear distance $\ClearDistance =$ `{python} StoppingBudget.d_clear_str` (illustrative).
* Pre-brake delay $\PrebrakeDelay =$ `{python} StoppingBudget.tau_delay_str` (derived). It is the sum of five registry terms: the observation age of the camera frame that first shows the worker, `{python} StoppingBudget.t_age_str`, which includes the `{python} StoppingBudget.t_backbone_str` perception backbone (the rest is half the exposure, sensor readout, transfer, image processing, and the handoff to the proposer, itemized in @sec-perception-latency-waterfall); the chunk lease of `{python} StoppingBudget.t_lease_str`, the longest an admitted command may drive before the permission path must act; one permission tick of `{python} StoppingBudget.t_tick_str`; one bus cycle of `{python} StoppingBudget.t_bus_str`; and a brake onset of `{python} StoppingBudget.t_onset_str`. It excludes the dispatch-to-admission interval, for the reason given with @eq-boundary-stopping-budget.

**Math**:

`{python} StoppingBudget.tau_sum_math`
`{python} StoppingBudget.blind_math`
`{python} StoppingBudget.brake_math`
`{python} StoppingBudget.close_math`
`{python} StoppingBudget.vstar_math`

**Result**: The elementary budget fits, with `{python} StoppingBudget.spare_str` to spare. The drive limit sits above the crossover speed, so braking dominates: it needs `{python} StoppingBudget.brake_over_blind_mult_str` the travel of the delay, and the delay adds `{python} StoppingBudget.blind_share_str` to the braking distance. At half speed, `{python} StoppingBudget.v_half_str`, delay travel halves to `{python} StoppingBudget.blind_half_str` while braking quarters to `{python} StoppingBudget.brake_half_str`, for a stop of `{python} StoppingBudget.d_stop_half_str`.

**Systems insight**: The learned model's backbone accounts for `{python} StoppingBudget.t_backbone_str` of the delay, or `{python} StoppingBudget.d_backbone_str` of travel; the chunk lease alone costs `{python} StoppingBudget.d_lease_str`. Each added millisecond of delay anywhere in the chain costs `{python} StoppingBudget.d_per_ms_str` at this speed, so a slower but more accurate model is a distance cost the budget must absorb. The spare is not yet a safety margin. @Sec-enforcement-composite-budget adds the localization bound, a protective margin, tracking error, and the longer stop of a jerk-limited brake (one that limits jerk, the rate of change of deceleration, by ramping its braking up instead of stepping it); together they exceed the clear distance at the drive limit, which is why the card sets the aisle speed at `{python} StoppingBudget.v_aisle_str`.

:::

::: {#fig-01-kinematic-roofline data-explore="guided-figure" data-explore-key="vol4:fig-01-kinematic-roofline" fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**Delay travel and braking travel against speed**: The elementary stopping budget of the loaded base, split into travel during the `{python} StoppingBudget.tau_delay_str` pre-brake delay, which grows linearly with speed, and braking travel at `{python} StoppingBudget.a_brake_str`, which grows with its square. The two terms are equal at the crossover speed $\StoppingCrossoverSpeed$; above it braking dominates. At the `{python} StoppingBudget.v_str` drive limit the elementary stop fits inside the `{python} StoppingBudget.d_clear_str` clear distance, before the allowances that later chapters add." fig-alt="Plot of distance in millimeters against speed from 0 to 2 meters per second. A straight line for travel during the delay and a rising parabola for braking travel cross at a marked crossover speed near 0.5 meters per second. Their sum rises more steeply and meets a dashed horizontal line marking the clear distance. A marked point at the drive limit of 1.5 meters per second sits on the sum curve below the line."}

```{python}
#| label: plot-01-kinematic-roofline
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ DELAY TRAVEL AND BRAKING TRAVEL AGAINST SPEED (FIGURE)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @fig-01-kinematic-roofline in @sec-boundary-kinematic-roofline
# │ Goal:    show the two terms of the elementary budget crossing at v*, and the
# │          drive-limit stop against the clear distance
# │ Show:    v tau_delay (133.6 ms), v^2/(2 a_brake) (2.0 m/s^2), their sum,
# │          D_clear 1.10 m, v* = 0.53 m/s, the 1.5 m/s point at 762.9 mm
# │ How:     StoppingBudget inputs over a speed grid; no value is retyped
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
import numpy as np
from mlsysim import viz
from mlsysim.fmt import check

SB = StoppingBudget
MPS = meter / second

# ┌── 1. LOAD (from boundary-stopping-budget) ─────────────────────────────────
tau = SB.tau_delay.to(second).magnitude
a = SB.a_brake.to(MPS / second).magnitude
d_clear = SB.d_clear.to(millimeter).magnitude
v_op = SB.v.to(MPS).magnitude
v_star = SB.v_star.to(MPS).magnitude
d_op = SB.d_stop.to(millimeter).magnitude

# ┌── 2. EXECUTE ──────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
v = np.linspace(0.0, 2.0, 401)
delay = v * tau * 1000.0
braking = v**2 / (2 * a) * 1000.0
total = delay + braking

# ┌── 3. GUARD ────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
check(abs(v_op * tau * 1000.0 + v_op**2 / (2 * a) * 1000.0 - d_op) < 1e-6, "The plotted point must equal the notebook's stop.")
check(abs(v_star * tau - v_star**2 / (2 * a)) < 1e-9, "The two terms must be equal at v*.")
check(d_op < d_clear, "The drive-limit point must sit below the clear distance.")

# ┌── 4. PLOT ─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
fig, ax, COLORS, plt = viz.setup_plot(figsize=(6.2, 4.2))
ax.plot(v, delay, color=COLORS["BrownLine"], lw=1.8, label=r"travel during the delay, $v\,\tau_{\mathrm{delay}}$")
ax.plot(v, braking, color=COLORS["BlueLine"], lw=1.8, label=r"braking travel, $v^2/(2a_{\mathrm{brake}})$")
ax.plot(v, total, color=COLORS["primary"], lw=2.0, label=r"elementary stop, $d_{\mathrm{stop}}$")
ax.axhline(d_clear, color=COLORS["RedLine"], lw=1.3, ls=(0, (6, 3)))
ax.text(0.04, d_clear + 30, f"clear distance {d_clear / 1000:.2f} m", color=COLORS["RedLine"], fontsize=9, va="bottom")
ax.plot([v_star], [v_star * tau * 1000.0], "o", ms=6, mfc="white", mec=COLORS["primary"], mew=1.4, zorder=5)
ax.annotate(
    f"$v^*$ = {v_star:.2f} m/s",
    xy=(v_star, v_star * tau * 1000.0),
    xytext=(v_star + 0.12, 25),
    fontsize=9,
    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=COLORS["primary"], lw=0.8),
)
ax.plot([v_op], [d_op], "o", ms=7, color=COLORS["primary"], zorder=5)
ax.annotate(
    f"drive limit {v_op:.1f} m/s: {d_op:.1f} mm",
    xy=(v_op, d_op),
    xytext=(v_op - 0.62, d_op + 170),
    fontsize=9,
    arrowprops=dict(arrowstyle="-", color=COLORS["primary"], lw=0.8),
    bbox=dict(boxstyle="square,pad=0.1", fc="white", ec="none"),
)
ax.set_xlim(0, 2.0)
ax.set_ylim(0, 1600)
ax.set_xlabel("Initial speed, $v$ (m/s)")
ax.set_ylabel("Distance (mm)")
ax.legend(loc="upper left", bbox_to_anchor=(0.0, 0.93), fontsize=9, frameon=False)
plt.tight_layout()
plt.show()
```
:::

The running machine's drive limit lies well above the crossover speed the notebook computed (@fig-01-kinematic-roofline), so braking, not delay, sets most of its stop, and the sum still clears the dashed clear-distance line before any later allowance is added. These values are representative parameters and a derived latency profile, not measured stopping distances for a real chassis, but they already show the two levers a designer holds. Shortening response latency contracts the linear term, whereas lowering cruising speed contracts both, the braking term quadratically. Selecting a model purely on offline accuracy overlooks the first lever, because added inference latency is added travel.

The budget just computed models one particular detection path, and naming it shows which learned computation it charges. The worker is seen by the learned perception stack, so the perception backbone sits inside the observation age. The chunk policy's own compute time does not appear, because the lease, not the policy, bounds how long an admitted chunk may keep driving once the proposer falls silent. A machine can also carry a second, independent protective path with its own sensing, timing, power, and fallback logic, such as a certified safety scanner wired to the drives. A stop that path triggers bypasses perception dispatch and the lease entirely. The backbone and lease terms leave its delay, and its own sensing and switching latency take their place, while the braking travel and the allowances stay. Under that decoupled architecture, the protective path's latency, rather than the execution time of the neural network, governs the protective stop. Industrial automated guided vehicles (AGVs) implement this separation today, with safety standards mandating certified safety scanners that halt the machine before human contact, independent of fleet management or guidance computers [@iso3691part4]. This book layers learned sensorimotor proposers atop deterministic safety kernels and analyzes the architectural contracts required between them.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ The scanner path's own timing budget, and how the software stopping budget maps onto certified safety functions, are developed in @sec-enforcement-certified-functions.
:::

Deploying this budget in real-world facilities requires several additional physical allowances. Beyond the allowances the notebook's systems insight names (localization, a protective margin, tracking error, and the longer jerk-limited stop), real-world controllers must also account for unmodeled initial acceleration and degraded tire-floor traction. Dynamic obstacles complicate the clearance budget even further: if a pedestrian walks toward the mobile robot at speed $\HumanWalkingSpeedBound$, the relative closing distance contracts during both the pre-brake delay and the mechanical deceleration phase. For this reason, functional safety standards mandate adding a pedestrian approach-speed allowance to the vehicle's own braking distance [@iso13855]. Later chapters formalize these dynamic constraints and allocate delay budgets across compute hardware. Even before they do, a learned policy's behavior is acceptable only inside the real-time envelope that plant momentum sets.

### Irreversibility and recovery {#sec-boundary-thermodynamic-irreversibility}

The stopping budget prices one consequence of irreversibility. The other is what recovery becomes. A database transaction that aborts restores the state it started from, but a gripper that has permanently deformed a workholding fixture, or a winding whose insulation has degraded from overheating, has no earlier state to return to. Recovery on a physical machine is therefore a new trajectory, not a reversal.

Corrective commands can brake the motors, release a grasp, or plan a diversion, but each is itself motion, limited by the torque the actuators can deliver, by friction, and by the speeds and accelerations the drives can reach. Which limit governs depends on what the machine is doing. For the mobile base it is stopping clearance under momentum. When the arm closes its jaws on a fragile component or braces against an assembly fixture, it is contact force, the flex of the gears and belts between motor and gripper (transmission compliance), and heat in the windings. Because recovery is constrained motion, the permission path must check before it admits an action that a feasible recovery from the resulting state will still exist; checking afterward is too late.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ The contact loads a transmission delivers to a gripped part or a latch, the arm's limiting quantity here, are developed in @sec-body-transmission-compliance.
:::

## Three Machine Classes {#sec-boundary-three-classes}

The physical constraints that govern an embodied system shift dynamically across its operating cycle. As the warehouse mobile manipulator travels down an aisle, its primary engineering challenge is kinetic, preserving sufficient clearance to stop safely before an obstacle. When pressing against a door latch, the governing constraint shifts to contact mechanics, regulating interaction forces to avoid damaging the mechanism or the workpiece. When holding a suspended payload stationary, the machine performs zero mechanical work, yet its actuators must sustain continuous stall torque without exhausting thermal headroom or browning out the shared electrical supply. Each regime spends a different physical margin, and the book names three machine classes by the margin each one spends (@fig-01-three-archetypes).

**Mass-dominated mobility** (Class 1) spends stopping clearance. A mobile base, delivery vehicle, or aerial drone carries significant momentum and cannot halt instantaneously. Forward velocity, control and sensing latency, and available braking deceleration or reverse thrust jointly dictate the spatial clearance required to arrest or redirect its motion.

**Contact-dominated manipulation** (Class 2) spends force and deformation margin. When an articulated arm presses against a stiff fixture, minute position displacements can generate destructive contact forces over fractions of a millimeter. Physical contact is both the means of task success (seating a part or opening a latch requires deliberate force) and the immediate hazard. The engineering task is to supply the wrenches (the combined forces and torques) needed to complete the assembly while guaranteeing that contact forces never exceed the mechanical yield limits of the payload or the manipulator.

**Energy- and thermal-dominated operation** (Class 3) spends heat and electrical supply margins. Supporting a heavy load or resisting gravity demands sustained motor current, driving continuous Joule heating in actuator windings even when joints remain stationary. Concurrent peak current draws from drive inverters, compute accelerators, and sensor payloads can induce voltage sag across a shared DC bus. The system must sustain these thermal and electrical loads across the entire operational profile while reserving sufficient energy and thermal headroom to execute a safe protective abort.

::: {#fig-01-three-archetypes data-explore="guided-figure" data-explore-key="vol4:fig-01-three-archetypes" fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Three machine classes**: Each class is named for the constraint that dominates it and the margin it spends: (a) mass-dominated mobility (Class 1) spends stopping clearance, set by momentum and braking; (b) contact-dominated manipulation (Class 2) spends force and deformation margin, set by contact stiffness and the strength of the object and mechanism; and (c) energy- and thermal-dominated operation (Class 3) spends heat and supply margin, set by Joule heating, thermal capacitance, and power delivery." fig-alt="Three panels. Class 1, mass-dominated mobility: a wheeled base moving at speed v toward a rack end, with the clear distance D clear marked in red, above the relation d stop equals v tau delay plus v squared over 2 a brake. Class 2, contact-dominated manipulation: an arm whose gripper presses a spring of stiffness k contact into a stiff fixture, deformation delta x and force F in red, above F approximately equals k contact delta x. Class 3, energy- and thermal-dominated: power P in entering a winding of thermal capacitance C th, heat P out leaving, and a temperature bar T wind below a red T limit line, above d T wind over d t equals P in minus P out over C th. Each panel names the margin it spends: stopping clearance, force and deformation margin, heat and supply margin."}
![](images/svg/fig01_three_archetypes.svg){width="100%"}
:::

These three classes identify dominant physical constraints rather than mutually exclusive hardware categories. A practical robot transitions across all three regimes throughout a single task. The running machine integrates a wheeled base, an articulated arm, navigation lidar, and wrist cameras. An end-to-end learned policy can coordinate simultaneous base trajectories and arm proposals [@fu2024mobile], but the integrated machine must enforce the safety envelopes of every regime concurrently. A fixed-base arm still faces thermal and bus-voltage limits during prolonged holding, just as a wheeled base encounters contact constraints when docking against a workstation.

::: {#capstone-boundary-humanoid-crucible .callout-perspective title="The humanoid crucible"}
A humanoid robot exposes the tight coupling across all three regimes. Catching a shifted load perturbs dynamic balance, requiring an immediate recovery step that demands peak joint torque. That torque surge draws heavy current from the shared DC bus and injects rapid thermal energy into the joint windings. If the power distribution network sags or thermal protection limits current, the recovery step fails and the machine falls. Shielding the onboard computing stack from reset does not by itself supply the transient mechanical energy needed to stabilize the body. The part-ending humanoid examples throughout this book test how each systems principle survives these tightly coupled physical demands.
:::

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ The multi-contact balance mechanics a humanoid's recovery step depends on are developed in @sec-appendix-control-centroidal.
:::

Whether a given physical deployment also requires the learned policies and delegated-authority architecture developed throughout this book is a separate question from which margin it spends, and the scope test of the next section answers it.

## The Physical AI Scope Test {#sec-boundary-scope-test}

A robotic arm in a fulfillment center can follow a fixed motion profile under a proportional-integral-derivative (PID) controller (a classical hand-tuned feedback law that corrects in proportion to the present error, its accumulated sum, and its rate of change), execute an offline trajectory pre-screened and loaded by a human technician, or stream joint torques directly from a learned policy running on real-time sensor frames. While all three regimes actuate identical electric motors and gear trains, they impose different architectural obligations on the computing system. The scope test establishes the operational boundaries that define physical AI throughout this book.

The scope of physical AI is defined by the simultaneous intersection of three structural criteria:

1. **Learned Statistical Model:** The system relies on a policy, perception encoder, or world model whose runtime behavior emerges from training data rather than an inspectable closed-form specification, as seen in deep neural networks or diffusion policies [@chi2024diffusionpolicy]. Correctness cannot be formally proven across all state configurations from source code alone; engineers must establish operational validity empirically across a defined operating domain. By contrast, a linear plant model fitted through classical system identification,[^fn-sysid-scope-test] where parameter uncertainty yields provable stability margins, falls outside this category. A high-capacity neural policy falls within it.
2. **Consequential Physical Feedback:** The system's actions alter the material state of the surrounding physical world, and those state changes directly govern what its sensors measure in subsequent time steps under classical mechanics, thermodynamics, or electromagnetism. The environment cannot be paused or rolled back, and energy dissipated into it cannot be recalled.
3. **Delegated Authority:** The system's outputs reach execution without synchronous human approval for each control cycle. In a machine that also meets the second criterion, that execution is actuation, so the authority is physical. A learned component holds this authority whenever its output (a raw percept, a semantic state estimate, or a proposed motion trajectory) can propagate to live actuators without such approval. The learned network need not write directly to motor driver registers; the system possesses delegated authority whenever learned signals actively shape downstream actuation commands. Adding downstream safety checks or deterministic rate limiters does not vacate this authority, provided accepted proposals still drive hardware motion.

Together, these three criteria delineate the domain of physical AI. The three-set Venn diagram in @fig-01-scope-venn formalizes this boundary, locating physical AI at the central intersection where a learned model, consequential physical feedback, and delegated authority converge. Each pairwise overlap holds systems that meet exactly two criteria. Advisory systems have a learned model inside a physical process that changes the world, but a person approves each action, as when a technician inspects learned toolpaths before loading them onto a mill. Digital autonomy has a learned model whose outputs execute without approval, but its actions land in software rather than in physics, as with an automated trading engine. Classical control has physical feedback and automatic actuation without a learned model, as with a PID speed governor. Excluding these pairwise overlaps restricts the design problem to systems where statistical uncertainty collides directly with physical irreversibility.

[^fn-sysid-scope-test]: **System Identification**: The control-engineering practice of fitting low-order dynamic models to measured input-output time series. When the identification procedure establishes bounded parameter uncertainty under stated modeling assumptions, control theorists can use those bounds to construct provable stability guarantees before deploying the controller. In contrast, modern high-dimensional neural representations lack tractable closed-form uncertainty bounds, requiring empirical verification across explicitly specified operational domains. \index{System identification!scope test}

::: {#fig-01-scope-venn data-explore="guided-figure" data-explore-key="vol4:fig-01-scope-venn" fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**The physical AI scope test**: Physical AI combines a learned component, consequential physical feedback, and delegated authority to let learned outputs reach actuation without human approval. An independent veto belongs inside this intersection because accepted proposals can still move the plant. The pairwise overlaps locate advisory systems, digital autonomy, and classical control." fig-alt="Three-set Venn diagram defining physical AI at the intersection of learned models, physical feedback, and delegated authority. The pairwise overlaps show advisory systems, digital autonomy, and classical control."}
![](images/svg/fig01_scope_venn.svg){width="90%"}
:::

A learned model alone does not make a machine a physical AI system. Consider an offline trajectory generator that optimizes smooth paths using a learned diffusion model. If a manufacturing engineer must inspect, validate, and load those toolpaths onto a CNC mill prior to cutting metal, the statistical model operates only as an advisory tool. The human retains ultimate physical authority. Similarly, a vision model that highlights defects on an assembly line display assists human inspection without closing the physical loop.

Conversely, delegated authority does not require end-to-end neural control. Most production autonomous systems adopt modular architectures where deep neural networks handle perception while deterministic trajectory planners compute actual actuator setpoints. These systems satisfy the delegated-authority test through perception: if an unvetted object detection or bounding-box estimate triggers an automated swerve or emergency braking maneuver, the learned representation directly dictates plant dynamics. The autonomous test vehicle in the Tempe collision examined in @sec-boundary-when-fails is such a machine: changing classifications in its modular perception fed the path predictions that decided whether it would brake.

Shared autonomy falls within physical AI whenever a learned sub-system modifies live motion before a human operator can intervene. In a robotic surgical console equipped with learned haptic virtual fixtures, for example, the assistive policy exerts real forces on the master tool manipulators to guide the surgeon around delicate anatomical structures. Even if the surgeon holds administrative responsibility for the procedure, high-bandwidth force cues alter physical tissue contact well within normal human neurological reaction latency (typically 150 ms to 250 ms). Because the machine enforces learned spatial guidance dynamically without requiring the surgeon to review and acknowledge each micro-correction, it exercises delegated authority over physical motion.

When classifying an ambiguous machine, engineers must evaluate each of the three criteria independently. Implementing an independent deterministic veto, such as an analog brake relay triggered by a certified safety lidar, does not strip a machine of delegated authority, because learned proposals still govern all nominal motion up to the intervention threshold. In contrast, requiring a human operator to screen and authorize every trajectory command before transmission reliably removes that authority. Once a design satisfies all three criteria, it qualifies as physical AI, and its computing architecture must respect the hard timing and causal boundaries established in @sec-boundary-causal-boundary.

- [ ] **Stopping budget estimate**: Using the machine card, estimate how far the elementary stop at the `{python} StoppingBudget.v_str` drive limit grows if the `{python} StoppingBudget.t_lease_str` chunk lease doubles, and determine whether it still fits inside the `{python} StoppingBudget.d_clear_str` clear distance.
- [ ] **Binding margins**: Identify the relevant physical margin when the warehouse machine travels, presses a latch, and holds a load.
- [ ] **Scope criteria**: Apply all three scope criteria to a new machine, including one whose learned output passes through an independent veto.

:::

Satisfying the scope test binds statistical uncertainty directly to hardware consequences. To design systems that operate safely under these demands, computer systems engineers must map how timing, state estimation, and control authority distribute along the execution path from raw sensor frames to physical actuator motion.

## The Machine in Five Levels {#sec-boundary-machine-model}

When the running machine's chunk policy stalls mid-aisle, something other than the policy must still be able to stop the base. When the policy emits a chunk that would carry the arm through a coworker's hand, something other than the policy must refuse it. An embodied machine therefore needs an architecture that prevents learned models from writing directly to the actuators they could damage, while still letting those models guide physical behavior.

The Body establishes what motion, force, and mechanical power the hardware can physically sustain. The Brain generates learned proposals intended to operate within those capabilities. Mediating between them, the Nervous System coordinates communication and control, preserving both the temporal margin and the hardware authority required to intercept and refuse an inadmissible command. Adding the interface where commands become current and the environment the machine acts on gives a five-level model that runs from learned computation down to the physical world:

1. **The Brain (Level 1):** The learned models that interpret sensory observations and propose candidate goals, trajectories, or torques. Generating a proposed trajectory or sequence of setpoints confers no intrinsic authority to execute it.
2. **The Nervous System (Level 2):** The deterministic communication buses, real-time schedulers, and control loops that bridge proposals to physical execution. Its permission path evaluates, filters, or rejects proposals against fresh sensory evidence and invariant physical limits, and it executes a fallback shown feasible from the current state under the stated sensing, plant, and response-time assumptions when the proposer falters.
3. **The Body (Level 3):** The physical plant, including motor drives, transmissions, electromagnetic windings, structural linkages, and energy storage, that delivers mechanical action.
4. **The Boundary (Level 4):** The hard physical and electrical interface where digital registers translate into actuator voltages or currents, and where physical phenomena register across sensor transducers as raw measurements.
5. **The World (Level 5):** The external physical environment (surfaces, payloads, obstacles, ambient lighting, and human collaborators), which evolves continuously under the laws of physics regardless of whether the machine measures it.

The list orders the levels by abstraction, from learned computation down to physics, not along the path a command travels. A command leaves the Nervous System, crosses the Boundary at a register write, and only then drives current through the Body's windings. The Boundary is listed after the Body because it gathers the transducers at both edges of the machine, the register writes that energize the windings and the sensor captures that turn light, force, and motion into numbers, and those are the places where the machine exchanges energy and information with the World. The actuation half of this level is the causal boundary defined earlier in the chapter. The proposal boundary, defined below, is not a level at all. It is the line between the Brain and the Nervous System that separates proposing from permitting.

A concrete physical AI implementation often maps this hierarchy across distinct computational tiers: learned proposers run on high-throughput accelerator hosts (such as an application processor paired with a GPU or neural processing unit), the permission path executes on an independent real-time microcontroller or dedicated real-time operating system (RTOS) core, and the current loops that regulate motor-phase current run directly on dedicated motor drives. This architectural isolation is rooted in strict timing guarantees and fault-containment boundaries rather than specific silicon families or nominal operating system labels.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ The loaded test of the two-processor split that realizes this isolation is developed in @sec-placement-testing-separation.
:::

Governance does not constitute a sixth level in this real-time control hierarchy. Instead, it serves as the operational and lifecycle envelope enclosing all five. Governance determines which entity holds valid command authority, what verification evidence licenses the machine to operate, and when that license lapses and must be renewed. Governance transitions unfold across the human and operational timescales of safety interventions, policy rollouts, and maintenance releases, rather than the millisecond rhythms of real-time control loops.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ The authority state machine that hands each actuator channel to exactly one owner during a transfer is developed in @sec-intervention-authority-transitions.
:::

::: {#dfn-boundary-proposal-boundary .callout-definition title="Proposal boundary"}

***Proposal boundary***\index{Proposal boundary!definition}\index{Permission path!definition} is the line between a learned model, which may only propose an action, and the **permission path**, an independent mechanism with bounded latency that the model cannot delay or corrupt and that alone may permit the action to reach an actuator. The permission path validates every proposal against fresh sensory evidence, the stopping envelope (the state space from which the machine can safely decelerate to a halt prior to obstacle collision), and a fallback trajectory shown feasible from the current state. On the running machine, the algorithmic admission checks remain an unrated performance layer (one not certified to a functional-safety rating) above separate certified protective functions; @sec-enforcement-certified-functions explains that distinction. If any condition is violated, the permission path rejects the proposal within the established response bound.

1.  **Significance**: Prevents learned model outputs from directly manipulating actuators. This architectural protection remains dependable only as long as the permission path's independent sensing, dynamic models, and fallback maneuvers remain physically valid.
2.  **Distinction**: Even a deep reinforcement learning policy trained to emit joint torques possesses zero raw actuator-write authority; its output remains a mere proposal until explicitly admitted by the permission path.
3.  **Common pitfall**: Treating the permission path as a cosmetic post-processing filter or output clamp, rather than an autonomous supervisory mechanism capable of seizing control when the learned proposer hangs, violates deadlines, emits pathological values, or falls silent.

The proposal boundary determines who holds the authority to approve an action, whereas the causal boundary marks the physical interface where an admitted command alters the state of the plant. The Nervous System bridges this divide, verifying proposals against hard constraints before energizing the drives.

:::

Readers steeped in classical control theory will recognize this design as a supervisory architecture. Specifically, the proposal boundary implements runtime assurance. In classic Simplex architectures, a complex, high-performance controller (here, the learned policy) is paired with a certified baseline controller, coordinated by decision logic that determines which subsystem drives the plant [@seto1998simplex; @sha2001using]. The lineage table in @sec-boundary-bedrock-laws (@tbl-01-law-lineage) maps this book's terms to their established names once the four laws are stated.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ Runtime assurance for physical AI, which pairs the learned proposer with a resident protective controller and an output selector, is developed in @sec-enforcement-deterministic-gatekeeper.
:::

Hardware fault isolation alone does not guarantee safety, because architectural independence also constrains the permission path's sensor inputs. The learned detection path used in the stopping budget prices response delay, but its lease cannot protect against a perception error that produces timely, unsafe proposals. If an enforcement monitor validates a proposed trajectory using the very same learned perception pipeline that synthesized it, a single perception error will corrupt both components simultaneously. The sensing pipelines that grant execution authority must therefore maintain distinct failure modes from the learned models they supervise.

@Fig-01-locator partitions the machine into five stacked architectural tiers, mapping each level to its characteristic control frequency and governing chapters: from the continuous physical World (bottom) up through the event-timed Boundary, the 10–25 kHz current loops of the mechanical Body, and the 1 kHz permission loops of the Nervous System, to the hierarchical Brain (operating from 40 Hz setpoints to 2 Hz intent models at the top). The prominent gap between Brain and Nervous System marks the foundational proposal boundary: components above this line may only formulate proposals, while only deterministic subsystems below it possess the authority to command physical actuators. The operating frequencies charted across the levels reflect the reference architecture analyzed throughout this book, rather than immutable physical constants for every robotic platform. Subsequent chapters derive these timing budgets directly from task dynamics and mechanical plant characteristics. What remains fundamental across all physical AI systems is the proposal boundary that severs learned computation from unchecked execution authority.

```{python}
#| label: boundary-locator-rates
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ LOCATOR RATES (LEGO GUARD FOR A HAND-DRAWN FIGURE)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @fig-01-locator (fig01_machine_levels.svg) in
# │          @sec-boundary-machine-model.
# │ Goal:    Keep the rates drawn on the Brain and Nervous System bands equal to
# │          the running machine's registry values.
# │ Show:    intent model 2 Hz; chunk renewal 20 Hz; setpoints 40 Hz; 1 kHz tick.
# │ How:     Read the registry; check() fails the build if a registry change
# │          leaves the SVG labels stale. Nothing prints.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim import *
from mlsysim.fmt import check

class LocatorRates:
    """Registry rates that fig01_machine_levels.svg draws as text."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    RM = Embodied.MobileManipulator.WarehouseMobileManipulator
    f_intent = RM.intent_rate.to(hertz).magnitude  # category: chosen
    f_chunk = RM.chunk_rate.to(hertz).magnitude  # category: chosen
    f_step = (1 / RM.chunk_step).to(hertz).magnitude  # category: derived from the chosen step
    f_tick = RM.permission_rate.to(hertz).magnitude  # category: chosen

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    drawn = {"intent": 2.0, "chunk": 20.0, "step": 40.0, "tick": 1000.0}  # labels in the SVG
    check(abs(f_intent - drawn["intent"]) < 1e-9, f"Locator draws intent at 2 Hz; registry says {f_intent}.")
    check(abs(f_chunk - drawn["chunk"]) < 1e-9, f"Locator draws chunk renewal at 20 Hz; registry says {f_chunk}.")
    check(abs(f_step - drawn["step"]) < 1e-9, f"Locator draws setpoints at 40 Hz; registry says {f_step}.")
    check(abs(f_tick - drawn["tick"]) < 1e-9, f"Locator draws a 1 kHz permission loop; registry says {f_tick}.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    # Guard-only class: it pins the values drawn in the figure; no prose outputs.
```

::: {#fig-01-locator data-explore="guided-figure" data-explore-key="vol4:fig-01-locator" fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**The five-level machine**: Each band carries its pinned rate and the chapters that work on it. The wider gap between Brain and Nervous System marks the proposal boundary, above which a component may only propose. A chapter-opening stack with no level highlighted marks a governance chapter. The permission-loop rate shown is one implementation." fig-alt="Five stacked horizontal bands labeled from top to bottom Brain (learned proposers, intent model 2 hertz, chunk renewal 20 hertz, setpoints 40 hertz), Nervous System (permission path, lease, fallback, a 1 kilohertz loop in one implementation), Body (drives, transmission, windings, rails, current loop 10 to 25 kilohertz), Boundary (register write and sensor capture, event-timed), and World (contact, friction, payload, people, continuous). A wider gap between Brain and Nervous System is labeled proposal boundary, above may only propose, below may command. A dashed outline enclosing all five bands is labeled governance, lifecycle envelope, Part IV, no control rate. Chapter numbers sit at the right edge of each band: Brain 3, 6, 8 to 11; Nervous System 4, 12, 13; Body 2; Boundary 1, 8; World 5, 7."}
![](images/svg/fig01_machine_levels.svg){width="100%"}
:::

Deploying capable physical AI requires balancing expressive policy proposals with deterministic execution guarantees. This separation of concerns does not demand rejecting every imperfect proposal out of hand; real-time intervention mechanisms can project a trajectory onto safe constraints or smoothly blend corrections, preserving task progress while respecting physical invariants. Systems evaluation must therefore disentangle what the learned proposer achieves in isolation, how effectively the integrated machine executes under routine supervisory filtering, and whether the fallback mechanisms themselves introduce secondary hazards.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ The minimal-intervention optimization filters that project a proposal onto its constraints are developed in @sec-enforcement-minimal-intervention.
:::

Distributing responsibilities across these five levels gives the rest of the book its structure. It also gives a way to diagnose real failures by asking which level failed, rather than reducing every physical malfunction to a deficiency in neural network weights.

## When the Responsibilities Fail Together {#sec-boundary-when-fails}

A warehouse model that recognizes an obstacle too late cannot recover the clearance already consumed. In a road vehicle, the same timing problem can combine with tracking errors, delayed intervention, and missing redundancy. The 2018 Tempe collision provides a documented example of these interacting failures; it does not establish that one prescribed hardware architecture would have prevented them. The National Transportation Safety Board (NTSB) attributed the crash primarily to the vehicle operator's distraction. The design choices traced below explain why the automated system had made that single, unmonitored person the last line of defense.

```{python}
#| label: boundary-incident-record
#| echo: false
#| warning: false
#| message: false
# ┌─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ THE TEMPE AND CRUISE RECORDS (LEGO)
# ├─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
# │ Context: @tbl-01-law-lineage and @sec-boundary-when-fails (Tempe timeline,
# │          action suppression, braking cap, Cruise pullover, checkpoint).
# │ Goal:    Print the investigators' own values once, and derive the travel
# │          during action suppression from the two recorded speeds.
# │ Show:    5.6 s first detection; 43.2 mph at 1.2 s before impact; 1 s
# │          suppression ending at 0.2 s and 40.5 mph; takeover at 0.02 s;
# │          18.7 m during suppression; 7 m/s^2 (0.71 g) chosen cap against
# │          0.92 g (9.0 m/s^2) capability; Cruise about 20 ft (6.1 m) at up
# │          to 7.7 mph.
# │ How:     Literature values from NTSB/HAR-19/03 and the Quinn Emanuel report,
# │          loaded here until the literature registry holds them. Suppression
# │          travel uses the mean of the two recorded speeds (trapezoid rule);
# │          no counterfactual stop is computed.
# └─────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────────
from mlsysim.core.units import *
from mlsysim.fmt import fmt, fmt_latency, fmt_length, fmt_velocity, fmt_acceleration, fmt_math, check

class IncidentRecord:
    """Investigator-reported values for the Tempe (2018) and Cruise (2023) cases."""

    # ┌── 1. LOAD (Constants & Parameters) ─────────────────────────────────
    # category: literature. NTSB/HAR-19/03 (2019), p. v and table pp. 15-16
    t_detect = 5.6 * second  # first detection, before impact
    t_recognize = 1.2 * second  # emergency recognized and suppression begins, before impact
    v_recognize = 43.2 * mph  # recorded speed at that instant
    t_suppress = 1.0 * second  # action-suppression period (p. 13)
    t_supp_end = 0.2 * second  # suppression ends, before impact
    v_supp_end = 40.5 * mph  # recorded speed at that instant
    t_takeover = 0.02 * second  # operator takes the wheel, before impact
    # category: literature. NTSB/HAR-19/03, p. 13 and footnote 33
    a_cap = 7.0 * meter / second**2  # ADS emergency threshold and braking cap (chosen by the developer)
    g_capable = 0.92  # police-determined average deceleration capability in the crash area, in g
    # category: literature. Quinn Emanuel report to the Cruise boards (2024), p. 10
    d_drag = 20 * foot  # approximate distance moved during the pullover
    v_drag = 7.7 * mph  # maximum speed during the pullover

    # ┌── 2. EXECUTE (Compute) ─────────────────────────────────────────────
    g0 = (1 * standard_gravity).to(meter / second**2)
    d_suppress = (0.5 * (v_recognize + v_supp_end) * t_suppress).to(meter)
    a_cap_g = (a_cap / g0).to("dimensionless").magnitude
    a_capable = (g_capable * g0).to(meter / second**2)
    d_drag_m = d_drag.to(meter)

    # ┌── 3. GUARD (Invariants) ───────────────────────────────────────────
    check(abs((t_recognize - t_supp_end - t_suppress).to(second).magnitude) < 1e-9, "Suppression must span the two table rows.")
    check(abs(a_cap_g - 0.71) < 5e-3, f"NTSB states the cap as 0.71 g, got {a_cap_g}.")
    check(a_capable > a_cap, "The chosen cap must sit below the vehicle's capability.")
    check(abs(d_suppress.magnitude - 18.7) < 0.05, f"Suppression travel is about 18.7 m, got {d_suppress}.")

    # ┌── 4. OUTPUT (Formatting) ──────────────────────────────────────────
    t_detect_str = fmt_latency(t_detect, unit=second, precision=1)
    t_suppress_str = fmt_latency(t_suppress, unit=second, precision=0)
    t_recognize_math = fmt_math(rf"\ImpactInstant-{fmt(t_recognize, unit=second, precision=1)}\text{{ s}}")
    t_supp_end_math = fmt_math(rf"\ImpactInstant-{fmt(t_supp_end, unit=second, precision=1)}\text{{ s}}")
    t_takeover_math = fmt_math(rf"\ImpactInstant-{fmt(t_takeover, unit=second, precision=2)}\text{{ s}}")
    v_recognize_str = fmt_velocity(v_recognize, unit=mph, precision=1)
    v_supp_end_str = fmt_velocity(v_supp_end, unit=mph, precision=1)
    d_suppress_str = fmt_length(d_suppress, unit=meter, precision=1)
    a_cap_str = fmt_acceleration(a_cap, unit=meter / second**2, precision=0)
    a_cap_g_str = fmt(a_cap_g, precision=2)
    g_capable_str = fmt(g_capable, precision=2)
    a_capable_str = fmt_acceleration(a_capable, unit=meter / second**2, precision=1)
    d_drag_str = fmt_length(d_drag, unit=foot, precision=0)
    d_drag_m_str = fmt_length(d_drag_m, unit=meter, precision=1)
    v_drag_str = fmt_velocity(v_drag, unit=mph, precision=1)
```

On a March night in 2018, a modified Volvo XC90 operating Uber Advanced Technologies Group's developmental automated driving system (ADS) struck and fatally injured a pedestrian pushing a bicycle across a road in Tempe, Arizona [@ntsb2019uber].[^fn-inc-tempe-investigation] The vehicle carried a roof-mounted lidar, forward and side radars, surround cameras, and GPS antennas, all routed to ADS compute and data-storage racks in the cargo bay (@fig-01-tempe-vehicle). The ADS first detected the pedestrian `{python} IncidentRecord.t_detect_str` before impact, but detection alone did not provide a correct path prediction [@ntsb2019uber]. The failure ran through perception and path prediction, a response rule that withheld braking, and a human operator the design relied on as its last countermeasure.

[^fn-inc-tempe-investigation]: **Reading the Tempe Record**\index{2018 Tempe Autonomous Collision!NTSB report}: Times in this section count backward from impact at $\Time$, as the event table of NTSB/HAR-19/03 does, and speeds are those the ADS itself recorded [@ntsb2019uber]. The report also cautions that communication delay leaves unclear exactly when the planned slowdown began. Reading each time as an interval before impact, rather than as a clock time, is what lets it be converted into distance traveled at the recorded speed, the conversion this section applies.

::: {#fig-01-tempe-vehicle fig-env="figure" fig-pos="t" fig-cap="**Tempe test vehicle sensor locations**: The NTSB diagram identifies the developmental ADS vehicle's lidar, camera, radar, computing, and telecommunications locations. (Source: NTSB, public domain)." fig-alt="NTSB side-view diagram of the Volvo test vehicle with colored outlines marking lidar, cameras, radar, ADS computing and data storage, and GPS equipment."}
![](images/jpg/fig01_real_ntsb_tempe_vehicle.jpg){width="95%"}
:::

### Tracking history loss under classification churn {#sec-boundary-tracking-churn}

Despite continuing to track the detected object, the ADS did not brake in response to it. The NTSB record shows classification changes among vehicle, bicycle, and other before `{python} IncidentRecord.t_recognize_math` [@ntsb2019uber].

When the classification changed, the ADS path predictor did not use the object's earlier locations; for an "other" object it could assume a static path.[^fn-ctrl-kalman-tracking] The loss of earlier locations matters because successive positions provide evidence of motion across the roadway. A changing semantic label must not silently discard that evidence. The resulting path predictions did not place the pedestrian in the SUV's lane until `{python} IncidentRecord.t_recognize_math` [@ntsb2019uber].

[^fn-ctrl-kalman-tracking]: **Tracking-History Loss**\index{Tracking history!classification changes}: The NTSB record states only that a changed classification caused the predictor to omit the object's earlier locations; it does not describe a Kalman-filter reset or a zero-velocity initialization, so neither should be read into it [@ntsb2019uber]. The consequence follows from the omission alone. Each relabeling shortened the evidence window from which motion is estimated, so an object crossing the lane began again, after each change, as one with no recorded history of crossing.

### Action suppression and the kinematic stopping deficit {#sec-boundary-action-suppression}

The ADS included an action-suppression interval intended to reduce responses to false alarms while the system checked the situation and allowed operator intervention [@ntsb2019uber]. That software choice also consumed time available for a physical response.

At `{python} IncidentRecord.t_recognize_math`, with the vehicle traveling at `{python} IncidentRecord.v_recognize_str`, the ADS recognized an emergency and entered its one-second action-suppression period. The design withheld braking while it checked the hazard or waited for operator intervention. At `{python} IncidentRecord.t_supp_end_math`, suppression ended with the vehicle at `{python} IncidentRecord.v_supp_end_str`. The ADS then initiated a plan for gradual slowdown and sounded an alert; it did not request emergency braking. The NTSB notes that communication delay leaves unclear whether that slowdown began before the operator disengaged the ADS at `{python} IncidentRecord.t_takeover_math` [@ntsb2019uber].

::: {.column-margin}
![](images/svg/margin_tempe_suppression_strip.svg){width="100%" fig-alt="A column of five stacked cells in time order from top to bottom, headed seconds before impact: detected at 5.6 seconds, emergency recognized at 1.2 seconds, a red cell for the one-second action suppression labeled 18.7 meters with the brake withheld, slowdown planned at 0.2 seconds, and operator takeover at 0.02 seconds. Cell heights are not to scale."}

*Recognition came seconds after detection; suppression then spent `{python} IncidentRecord.d_suppress_str` with the brake withheld.*
:::

The first term of the warehouse stopping budget applies directly. Averaging the two recorded speeds over the `{python} IncidentRecord.t_suppress_str` of suppression, the vehicle traveled about `{python} IncidentRecord.d_suppress_str` while emergency braking was withheld, distance that no later action could recover. The speed still fell during that second because a slowdown for the planned right turn at the next intersection was already under way; what the suppression withheld was the emergency response [@ntsb2019uber]. The emergency itself was defined by a chosen limit. The ADS treated a situation as an emergency when avoiding a collision required more than `{python} IncidentRecord.a_cap_str` (`{python} IncidentRecord.a_cap_g_str` g) of deceleration or a jerk[^fn-jerk-brake-ramp] beyond its limit, and it capped its own automated braking at that deceleration; police determined that the vehicle could decelerate at an average of `{python} IncidentRecord.g_capable_str` g, about `{python} IncidentRecord.a_capable_str`, on that road surface [@ntsb2019uber]. The difference between a chosen permission limit and a physical one is the distinction the book's numbers keep throughout. The calculation stops short of a counterfactual stop, because the report does not establish when a different design would have begun braking. Detection, correct path prediction, hazard recognition, and physical braking are distinct events; reporting the first detection time alone conceals the failures between them.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ The stopping envelope, which charges every interval of delayed braking against the clear distance, is developed in @sec-enforcement-stopping-envelopes.
:::

[^fn-jerk-brake-ramp]: **Jerk Limit**: Jerk, met in the stopping notebook as the rate of change of deceleration, is measured in m/s³. A jerk limit makes a brake ramp its deceleration up instead of stepping it, which spares occupants, loads, and transmissions a shock but costs stopping distance, because full deceleration arrives later. The warehouse machine's card carries a jerk bound for the same reason, and the machine's finished stopping budget pays for the ramp. \index{Jerk!braking}

::: {#ws-boundary-missing-safety-referee .callout-war-story title="The disabled safety redundancy (2018)"}
**Context**: On March 18, 2018, a developmental ADS on a 2017 Volvo XC90 struck and killed a pedestrian crossing a road in Tempe, Arizona [@ntsb2019uber].

**Mechanism**: As traced above, classification changes discarded the object's tracking history, and the one-second suppression withheld braking until only a gradual slowdown was planned. The design did not use maximum braking solely to mitigate an unavoidable collision [@ntsb2019uber].

**Impact**: The vehicle struck and fatally injured the pedestrian. The late gradual-slowdown plan could not recover the lost stopping opportunity.

**Response**: The NTSB determined that the probable cause was the vehicle operator's failure to monitor the driving environment and the ADS because she was visually distracted throughout the trip by her personal cell phone. It found three contributing factors at Uber ATG, all a consequence of an inadequate safety culture: inadequate safety risk assessment procedures, ineffective oversight of vehicle operators, and a lack of adequate mechanisms for addressing operators' automation complacency. The impaired pedestrian's crossing outside a crosswalk and the Arizona Department of Transportation's insufficient oversight of automated vehicle testing also contributed. The NTSB further found that deactivating the Volvo collision warning and automatic emergency braking, which Uber ATG had done over possible radar interference, removed a layer of safety redundancy, and it recommended stronger safety risk management for testing automated vehicles [@ntsb2019uber].

**Systems lesson**: Classification uncertainty, a delayed response rule, and reliance on an inattentive operator can combine. The design made the operator the primary countermeasure in an emergency, yet no mechanism monitored her attention in real time: authority rested on evidence nobody collected. A design needs timely hazard assessment and a response that can mitigate impact when avoidance is no longer possible; the investigation does not prescribe a particular hardware architecture.
:::

The investigation supports a broader architectural requirement. A developmental ADS needs safety redundancy and a timely mitigation path even when perception or path prediction fails, and simulation tests by Volvo that the NTSB cites suggest that the factory emergency braking might have prevented or mitigated this collision. The report does not establish when a separate permission path would have triggered or where it would have stopped the vehicle.[^fn-std-safety-standards]

[^fn-std-safety-standards]: **Safety-Critical Standards**\index{Safety-Critical Standards!autonomous systems}: Three standards divide the ground. ISO 26262 addresses hazards caused by faults in a vehicle's electrical and electronic systems [@iso26262]; ISO 21448, safety of the intended functionality (SOTIF), addresses hazards that arise when a function works as designed but performs insufficiently, as perception can [@iso21448]; and UL 4600 sets out the safety case for autonomous products with no human driver to fall back on [@ul4600]. Tempe falls on the SOTIF side, since the recorded failures were in classification and path prediction rather than in a faulted component, and none of the three prescribes a processor architecture. @Sec-release-standards-map maps the standards that govern the running machine.

Tempe illustrates failure *before* impact, where classification changes and a software suppression delay prevented timely braking. The 2023 Cruise robotaxi incident marks the opposite pole *after* impact. A hit-and-run driver's car threw a pedestrian into the path of the driverless vehicle, which braked hard but struck her and stopped. It then began a pullover toward a minimal-risk condition[^fn-mrc-fallback-motion] and, because its sensing did not detect a person beneath the vehicle, moved about `{python} IncidentRecord.d_drag_str` (`{python} IncidentRecord.d_drag_m_str`) at up to `{python} IncidentRecord.v_drag_str` while she was pinned beneath it. This account comes from a review commissioned by the company's boards, whose focus was the company's disclosures to regulators [@quinnemanuel2024cruise].

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ The Cruise pullover, and the fallback rule that forbids renewed motion while the space beneath the vehicle is unverified, are developed in @sec-enforcement-four-rungs.
:::

[^fn-mrc-fallback-motion]: **Minimal-Risk Condition**: In automated driving, the stable, usually stopped, state a system brings a vehicle to when a trip cannot or should not continue. Reaching it can itself require motion, as a pullover to the curb does, and in the Cruise case that motion was the harm. A fallback trajectory therefore needs the same permission check as any other proposal, judged against fresh evidence about the space it will move through. \index{Minimal-risk condition!fallback motion}

Neither failure reduces to an inaccurate model. The first spent stopping distance before braking began, and no later action could recover it. The second chose motion after the impact without fresh evidence about the space it moved through. Together they show what must hold before the machine acts and what a fallback may do once harm has begun. Both also had to be reconstructed afterward from records of what the machine perceived and when, so accountability, like safety, depends on the path that authorizes motion.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ Who answered for the Cruise collision, and the decisions behind an admitted action that no per-tick log records, are developed in @sec-responsibility-who-answered.
:::

::: {#chk-boundary-forensic-failure .callout-checkpoint title="Forensics of boundary and authority failures"}

Verify how the Tempe mechanisms connect to the architecture:

- [ ] **Classification changes and path prediction**: Explain how classification changes caused the ADS path predictor to omit earlier object locations, despite continued tracking.
- [ ] **Software suppression vs. kinematic clearance**: Distinguish the `{python} IncidentRecord.t_recognize_math` recognition time from the one-second suppression period, and explain why the gradual-slowdown plan at `{python} IncidentRecord.t_supp_end_math` could not restore the time already spent.
- [ ] **Safety redundancy**: Explain why disabling factory collision warning and emergency braking removed a layer of protection from a developmental ADS.

:::

## Safety Convergence {#sec-boundary-safety-convergence}

Tempe and Cruise both turned on what the machine knew when it moved or failed to brake, and both had to be reconstructed afterward from what it had recorded. The same three questions (whether the evidence behind a motion was sound, whether anything could refuse it, and whether the decision can be traced) also describe an attack and an audit. In enterprise software and distributed systems, safety, security, and accountability usually live in separate tiers. Security defends network boundaries with cryptographic tokens, reliability frameworks mitigate component failures through retries and circuit breakers, and accountability records transactions to append-only databases. In physical AI, all three converge on the causal boundary, the interface where software commands meet physical actuators. Consider the running machine crossing a warehouse aisle. It needs a valid stopping decision whether its forward cameras are obscured by dirt, an attacker has injected spoofed packets onto its internal Controller Area Network (CAN) bus, or a vision-language-action policy has hallucinated an unobstructed path. In each case the hazard is kinetic, a collision with racking or a worker. Because momentum cannot be rolled back like a failed database transaction, admission control cannot simply confirm who dispatched a command. It must determine whether executing that command now would violate the machine's physical limits.

An ordinary environmental change challenges this boundary as directly as an attack. The running machine's credible deceleration of `{python} StoppingBudget.a_brake_str` rests on the premise, stated on its card, that the floor supplies a friction coefficient of at least `{python} MachineCard.mu_all_str`. When the floor cannot supply the friction the brakes ask for, traction rather than the brakes caps deceleration, and braking distance grows in inverse proportion to the available friction. Spilled hydraulic fluid can drop tire-floor friction from about $0.8$ on dry concrete to $0.2$ (an illustrative pair). A vehicle that brakes at the traction limit would see its braking distance quadruple. The running machine asks far less of a dry floor than it supplies, but $0.2$ falls below its premise, so its credible deceleration no longer holds, and every clearance envelope and speed profile computed from that deceleration a moment earlier is invalid. The learned planner, processing camera streams that do not reveal the transparent slick, may continue to output an aggressive velocity command with high nominal confidence. Safety verification cannot treat the model's internal confidence as proof of physical feasibility. Restricting the machine requires independent, real-time evidence from the plant and its surroundings, such as wheel-slip telemetry, disagreement between commanded and inertial-measurement-unit (IMU) acceleration, and motor current transients, to detect the divergence and restrict motion using a response feasible under the updated traction estimate. If the machine has already consumed the clearance that response needs, detection can support harm mitigation but cannot establish collision avoidance.

Security threats target this same permission machinery by corrupting the evidence used to authorize motion. An adversary does not need to crack cryptographic keys or modify model weights to destabilize a physical agent; distorting the sensory inputs that inform admission decisions is sufficient. Projecting structured light patterns onto camera lenses, spoofing ultra-wideband (UWB) localization beacons, or injecting rogue packets into sensor buses can deceive the controller into approving destructive commands, even while the neural network executes its inference pipeline without numerical fault. Isolating the proposer from the permission path offers little defense if both subsystems ingest the same corrupted telemetry. Securing the causal boundary therefore requires validating the evidence itself, by cross-checking heterogeneous sensor streams (for example, corroborating camera-based visual odometry against wheel encoders and inertial sensors), enforcing cryptographic message authentication across bus transceivers, and maintaining fail-operational plausibility checks that reject sensor readings deviating from physical conservation laws.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ A well-formed packet that carries a false measurement becomes a fault trial in the injection campaign developed in @sec-verification-transduction-attacks.
:::

In digital systems, a cryptographic capability token or access control list entry grants authority to modify a file regardless of processor load or ambient conditions. In physical AI, **physical authority is state-dependent**. Cryptographic credentials establish identity and organizational rights to request an action, but physical admissibility depends entirely on the instantaneous operational state of the machine and its workspace. A joint velocity command of 2 rad/s may represent a routine transit when an industrial manipulator operates in open free space, yet that identical command becomes unacceptable if the arm is within 2 mm of a mechanical hard stop or a human coworker.
