Evaluating physical authority requires testing the proposed action against instantaneous kinematics, payload inertia, motor thermal headroom, and state estimation uncertainty. Admission control must also remain coupled to an executable fallback. If the permission gate rejects a proposed command because the machine approaches an operational boundary, the controller must immediately dispatch a dynamically feasible contingency maneuver, such as controlled regenerative braking or a compliant hold that yields to contact, that halts or redirects the plant without exceeding mechanical stress limits.

Accountability demands an audit trail that reconstructs the causal chain connecting sensory evidence to physical outcomes. When an embodied machine causes a collision or near-miss, post-incident analysis requires timestamp and clock-conversion uncertainty small enough to distinguish the relevant sensing, admission, dispatch, and physical-response events across multiple data streams: the raw observations ingested by the planner, the action proposed by the learned policy, the state estimates and dynamic constraints evaluated by the admission gate, the filtered command dispatched to the motor drives, and the measured response from joint encoders and force-torque sensors. Command logs record the intended trajectory, while sensor telemetry measures the plant's actual mechanical response. Recording dispatched setpoints alone does not confirm that an actuator executed them; an open-circuit fault, a tripped thermal breaker, or mechanical gearbox jamming will cause the physical plant to diverge immediately from commanded behavior. Both streams must be logged against synchronized hardware clocks (such as the IEEE 1588 Precision Time Protocol) so that investigators can distinguish between a planning failure, an admission gate error, and an electromechanical actuator breakdown. Reconstruction is necessary but does not by itself say who answers for an action, because the decisions that set the machine's envelope, its staffing, and its permission to operate are made before any tick and have to be recorded on purpose (@sec-responsibility-many-hands).

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ **Protocol:** The IEEE 1588 Precision Time Protocol exchange that aligns these clocks is developed in @sec-appendix-systems-ptp.
:::

Safety, security, and accountability ultimately converge on three unified demands at the permission path guarding the causal boundary:

1. **Fresh, authenticated physical state**: The permission gate must operate on telemetry fresh enough to bound physical uncertainty and robust enough against tampering or degradation to justify admitting an action.
2. **Deterministic authority to intervene**: The admission mechanism needs uncompromised physical authority to veto or clamp infeasible proposals and inject safe contingency maneuvers, regardless of the learned model's internal confidence or identity.
3. **Synchronized causal telemetry**: The system must keep an immutable record of what was proposed, what state was evaluated, what commands were dispatched, and how the machine responded.

The incidents above map onto these demands. Tempe's predictor discarded evidence it already had, and the factory emergency braking that could have intervened independently had been disabled; Cruise moved without fresh evidence about the space beneath it. Both investigations then depended on the third demand, the recorded telemetry from which the events were reconstructed. The permission path is therefore where a physical machine's safety, security, and accountability obligations are discharged, and anchoring probabilistic proposals to checks against physical limits is what lets learned capability operate within justified bounds. What those checks must respect, and why, is the subject of four laws.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ The operational log that survives physical failure, from which an investigator reconstructs each admitted action, is developed in @sec-intervention-trustworthy-logs.
:::

## The Four Bedrock Laws {#sec-boundary-bedrock-laws}

Manipulating an unfamiliar door latch or transporting an unmodeled payload requires far more than a sequence of statistically accurate model predictions. An embodied machine must respect the mechanical limits of its plant, adapt to dynamic environments altered by its own motion, and arbitrate between speculative model outputs and physically safe actuation. Four bedrock laws organize these engineering responsibilities, each anchoring a major part of this book:

**The first law: irreversibility.** Software cannot roll back physical consequences. In pure digital systems, an erroneous transaction can be aborted and state restored from a checkpoint. In physical space, however, work performed on a plant is thermodynamic and permanent. A motor command that collides with a fixture, tears a cable, or fractures a fragile payload cannot be retracted. Every admissibility check must therefore complete before the machine consumes its remaining clearance margin. As the stopping distance budget demonstrates, processing latency directly expends physical clearance, forcing the mechanical actuators to brake over an ever-shrinking distance. Reversing a drive voltage may eventually return an arm to its starting coordinates, but it cannot mend cracked structural material or recover energy lost to friction and heat. Part I translates this physical reality into kinetic budgets for the robot's body and deterministic timing constraints for its low-level controllers.

**The second law: endogenous data.** In classic offline machine learning, data samples are drawn independently from a stationary distribution. In embodied systems, data generation is endogenous. Every control action alters the physical state and determines what sensors will observe next. If an arm nudges an object during an approach, the object shifts; if a mobile base drifts off its nominal path, the subsequent visual frames deviate from the training demonstrations. Single-step prediction accuracy on an offline benchmark cannot guarantee closed-loop behavior, because minor execution errors compound across the task horizon, the covariate shift met with the closed causal loop (@sec-boundary-tensors-to-silicon). Part II frames data collection, model training, and policy evaluation as a continuous improvement cycle: diagnose behavioral failures, curate targeted recovery demonstrations, retrain candidate policies, and systematically evaluate both performance gains and unintended regressions. Empirical evidence from past rollouts bounds what can be claimed about present capability; only qualified new experience can expand that envelope.

**The third law: proposal is not permission.** A learned model operates only as a proposer, never as an unconstrained executor. An architecturally independent permission path (a runtime safety filter or an assurance monitor, for example) must arbitrate every proposed control command before that command reaches hardware actuators. Granting permission requires three prerequisites: fresh state estimates from verified sensors, an explicit check that the command respects every physical safety envelope, and an immediately executable fallback maneuver if the proposal is delayed, missing, or unsafe. This separation of authority must remain robust against system faults, so a runaway or stalled model thread must never be allowed to delay, starve, or corrupt the deterministic safety logic guarding the plant. Part III constructs the real-time execution runtime around this division between speculative proposal and independent, bounded permission.

**The fourth law: permission must be earned.** An embodied machine earns permission to operate only as far as empirical evidence supports its performance under stated conditions. Flawless execution across a handful of laboratory trials does not justify autonomy across diverse surface friction, variable payloads, degraded lighting, or sensor degradation. Every deployment safety case must explicitly demarcate the system's operational design domain (ODD),[^fn-odd-evidence-scope] articulate the environmental assumptions underlying those boundaries, and specify fail-safe degradation policies whenever runtime conditions drift beyond verified bounds. The 2018 Tempe collision showed the cost of ignoring this boundary. The system architecture relied on an in-vehicle safety operator as the primary emergency countermeasure, yet lacked any mechanism to monitor whether the operator was actually attending to the roadway [@ntsb2019uber]. Part IV formalizes command authority, fault injection testing, and release criteria so that epistemic and physical uncertainty bound what the machine is permitted to do.

[^fn-odd-evidence-scope]: **Operational Design Domain (ODD)**: The automated-driving name for the stated environmental and operational conditions (roadway types, speed ranges, weather, lighting) under which a system is designed to operate, and the foundational scope of a UL 4600 safety case [@ul4600]. This book applies the concept to the payloads, surface friction, operating velocities, and dynamic disturbances covered by the machine's empirical validation. Operating outside that verified domain rests on no evidentiary basis whatever, which is why @sec-data-curse-dimensionality-recoverability-geometry structures the operating domain as an explicit scenario table against which collected training data are audited. \index{Operational design domain!evidence}

Of these four, only the first is a physical law. Irreversibility follows from Newtonian mechanics and thermodynamics. Work performed on a plant transfers energy and raises entropy, and no software architecture can undo that transition. The remaining three are engineering design principles, distilled from decades of systems engineering, industrial robotics, and aerospace failures. A team could build an architecture that violates them, for example by piping unvalidated network outputs straight to motor amplifiers, but it would incur severe and predictable risks. The book elevates all four to bedrock laws because it treats them as mandatory constraints for any production embodied system.

None of these three architectural principles is entirely novel. Each has a rich foundation in computer systems, control theory, and safety-critical engineering. @Tbl-01-law-lineage maps this book's terminology to the established literature, alongside the canonical sources and documented real-world failures each principle distills, including the Tempe and Cruise incidents. Where the book's terms introduce tighter operational precision, as when tying state freshness directly to the dynamic stopping budget, the book retains specialized systems phrasing; when searching broader engineering literature, the classical terms serve as the standard index.

| Book's law or term                                                         | Kind             | Established name in the field                                             | Canonical source                                               | Documented failure it distills                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                         |
|:---------------------------------------------------------------------------|:-----------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------------------|:---------------------------------------------------------------|:-----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|
| First law: irreversibility (the causal boundary)                           | Physical         | Irreversible work on the plant; the reaction-plus-braking stopping budget | Mechanics; @sec-body-kinetic-momentum                          | Tempe (2018): the one-second action suppression let the vehicle travel about `{python} IncidentRecord.d_suppress_str` with emergency braking withheld [@ntsb2019uber]                                                                                                                                                                                                  |
| Second law: endogenous data                                                | Design principle | Covariate shift; compounding error in imitation learning                  | Ross, Gordon, and Bagnell [@ross2011reduction]                 | A learning result rather than an accident: a cloned policy's errors can compound with the task horizon (@sec-data-covariate-shift)                                                                                                                                                                                                                                     |
| Third law: proposal is not permission (proposal boundary, permission path) | Design principle | Runtime assurance and its Simplex architecture; safety filter             | Sha [@sha2001using]; Hsu, Hu, and Fisac [@hsu2024safetyfilter] | Therac-25: software took over protection that hardware interlocks had provided [@leveson1993investigating]; Mars Pathfinder (1997): through priority inversion, lower-priority work delayed a deadline-critical bus task until the scheduler's completion check reset the computer [@reeves1997pathfinder]                                                             |
| Fresh evidence (an input to every permission check)                        | Design principle | Age of information                                                        | Kaul, Yates, and Gruteser [@kaul2012realtime]                  | While not a pure staleness failure, Tempe (2018) shows the neighboring hazard of discarded evidence: each object reclassification dropped historical tracks, forcing path prediction to compute trajectories on truncated sensor history [@ntsb2019uber]                                                                                                               |
| Fourth law: permission must be earned                                      | Design principle | Assurance case; operational design domain (ODD)                           | UL 4600 [@ul4600]                                              | Tempe (2018): the design made the operator the primary countermeasure in an emergency, yet nothing monitored her attention in real time [@ntsb2019uber]; Cruise (2023): a post-collision pullover moved the vehicle without evidence that the space beneath it was clear, because its detection system did not identify the pedestrian there [@quinnemanuel2024cruise] |

: **Lineage of the four laws**: Each law and key term of this book against the field's established name, its canonical source, and a documented failure it distills. Only the first law is physical; the other three are design principles, which is why each has an independent literature. Runtime assurance enters with the proposal boundary, and @sec-boundary-history traces its lineage together with the safety filter and the assurance case. {#tbl-01-law-lineage tbl-colwidths="[20,10,20,16,34]"}

The proposal boundary is where the four laws meet in one architecture. Irreversibility requires that checks complete before a command alters the plant. Endogenous data explains why offline training metrics cannot certify the proposer, so its outputs must be checked in the closed loop. Proposal is not permission places that check outside the model, on a permission path the model cannot delay or corrupt. Permission must be earned confines admitted proposals to the conditions that evidence has verified.

Scaling up model capacity does not relax these constraints; on the contrary, it intensifies physical pressure on the system. Although general machine learning methods deliver superior performance as compute expands [@sutton2019bitter], the running mobile machine must supply its onboard compute within a finite electrical and thermal budget. Every additional neural layer, attention head, or diffusion step draws against fixed physical allocations of memory bandwidth, electrical power, and thermal dissipation. Inference latency on the stopping path is travel that braking cannot recover. On the running machine at its drive limit, each millisecond costs `{python} StoppingBudget.d_per_ms_str` of clearance, as the stopping notebook showed. This compute, thermal, and temporal ceiling forms the physical wall confronting every learned proposer.

::: {.column-margin .margin-pointer}
↪ The memory-bandwidth and latency bottlenecks confronting onboard learned proposers are developed in @sec-brain-cognitive-pipeline.
:::

Finally, rejecting an inadmissible command must have an explicit physical realization. In traditional software, an unhandled exception or failed assertion can simply terminate a thread. On a moving robot, halting a software process leaves physical momentum untouched. A refusal is meaningful only if the execution runtime immediately dispatches an admissible fallback (a dynamic braking maneuver, a compliant hold, or a controlled stop) that the physical body can safely execute within its remaining stopping clearance. Translating the four laws and their runtime mechanisms into an engineered system takes the four parts of this book, each producing records that later parts rely on.

## The Architecture of This Book {#sec-boundary-book-architecture}

Moving a learned proposal, such as the running machine's trajectory to open a warehouse cage door, from an abstract task requirement to safe, justified physical operation requires a disciplined four-stage progression. The engineer must first bound what the hardware plant can physically achieve, characterize what the learned proposer has demonstrated under rigorous testing, build an isolated runtime monitor to intercept live proposals, and establish the operational conditions under which continued execution remains justified. Each stage corresponds to one of the four laws. The system of records illustrated in @fig-01-spine formalizes this progression, capturing operating assumptions and empirical evidence so that downstream runtime decisions can inspect and rely on them. Conceptually, these records trace two converging pipelines. One strand establishes offline physical limits and verified competence; the second processes online sensor observations and real-time candidate actions. Both pipelines converge at the permission decision, where the system admits or rejects a proposed trajectory. In @sec-frontier-architectural-synthesis, this architecture synthesizes both strands to resolve the book's central challenge of engineering dependable, high-performance physical systems out of unverified learned models and unforgiving mechanical hardware.

A record is a machine-checkable artifact that downstream safety and runtime decisions can verify and trust. The initial stopping calculation (notebook \ref{nbk-boundary-stopping-budget}) already sketches the first record in the chain: a limit record, with the six elements the reader guide introduces (nominal value, operating conditions, uncertainty, margin, runtime detector, and provenance). Its nominal value is the derived stopping distance. Its operating conditions specify the payload mass, dry concrete, a stationary obstacle, and a constant approach speed. At this stage, however, its uncertainty remains unquantified because the inputs are illustrative scalars rather than calibrated empirical distributions. Consequently, the apparent buffer between the obstacle and the machine is simply an arithmetic difference between provisional figures rather than a verified safety margin. The system also lacks a runtime detector; no sensor on the machine currently monitors whether floor traction drops or cargo shifts outside the assumed envelope. @Sec-body-limit-record-schema specifies the runtime detector a limit record requires. Finally, its provenance consists solely of baseline assumptions rather than calibrated hardware logs. An ungrounded calculation becomes operational engineering evidence only when all six fields are populated and backed by empirical data. Every numbered box across the four part bands in @fig-01-spine establishes a machine-checkable record of this rigor for a distinct architectural decision.

::: {#fig-01-spine data-explore="guided-figure" data-explore-key="vol4:fig-01-spine" fig-env="figure" fig-pos="htb" fig-cap="**The spine of the book**: Each part is led by one law, and each chapter of Parts I to IV except The Cognitive Brain (Chapter 3) produces a record that a later one consumes. What the plant can do and what the proposer has shown it can do run as one strand, what the proposer proposes now as another, and the two meet at the permission decision." fig-alt="Flow diagram of sixteen record boxes, each labeled with its chapter number, on shaded bands for the four parts. In the Part I band, labeled Irreversibility, the limit record of Chapter 2 feeds the handoff record of Chapter 4, and a dashed arrow labeled Chapter 3, proposer limits, also enters the handoff record. The handoff record forks into two rows. The upper row, in the Part II band labeled Endogenous data, runs provenance record 5, policy manifest 6, and evaluation record 7. The lower row, in the Part III band labeled Proposal is not permission, runs observation contract 8, belief record 9, intent lease 10, and trajectory record 11. Both rows converge on the enforcement record of Chapter 12, which feeds the placement record of Chapter 13. An arrow then runs down to a lower row in the Part IV band, labeled Permission must be earned: authority record 14, fault record 15, release manifest 16, and approval record 17, which feeds the residual-claims register of Chapter 18 outside the bands. A separate arrow runs from the evaluation record around the top and right edges to the release manifest."}
![](images/svg/fig01_book_spine.svg){width="100%"}
:::

Part I, The Machine Anatomy, translates physical irreversibility into rigid architectural limits. @Sec-body profiles the mechanical plant to quantify its physical budgets (measurement freshness, stopping distance, deliverable torque, winding heat, and supply voltage). @Sec-brain measures the throughput and inference latency of the learned proposer, determining what it can deliver before deadlines expire. @Sec-nervous links compute to the actuators across deterministic buses, structuring a permission path whose timing guarantees derive from the plant's stopping requirements. The limit record and handoff record make every physical and temporal assumption explicit. Part II, Teaching the Machine, confronts the reality that physical actions continuously alter future sensor observations. @Sec-data, @sec-training, and @sec-evaluation build the evidentiary chain required to collect demonstrations, train control policies, and bound policy performance to a declared operational design domain. Across this pipeline, the provenance record, policy manifest, and evaluation record document both the empirical competence demonstrated by the model and the operational boundaries where its statistical guarantees break down.

Part III, Running the Machine, operationalizes the separation between proposing an action and permitting it to execute. From @sec-perception through @sec-placement, candidate commands are traced through the online runtime: qualifying sensor measurements in observation contracts, maintaining state estimates in a belief record, bounding a goal with an intent lease (a time-limited grant of a target, never of a path, and distinct from the chunk lease that bounds one motion segment), and checking candidate trajectories against real-time physical constraints before admission and dispatch, then testing whether the hardware keeps the permission path independent. Part IV, Governing the Machine, enforces the principle that permission must be earned. @Sec-intervention, @sec-verification, and @sec-release design the mechanisms that govern ongoing operation: transferring authority between the machine and a human operator, injecting faults to test whether protective responses work, and codifying deployment decisions in release manifests. @Sec-responsibility names who answers for each decision behind an admitted action, tests whether each human role the design relies on is one a person can perform, and counts the people who bear the machine's risk and appear in its records. @Sec-frontier brings the framework to bear on an unfamiliar machine, synthesizing what an engineering team can construct and formally justify while identifying the residual risks that require further mitigation. Across these parts, the warehouse mobile manipulator introduced here provides a single concrete machine on which to ground each architectural decision. Its records render design assumptions fully inspectable, though an engineer must remember that assembling a record documents an explicit claim rather than guaranteeing its physical truth. The system record register in @sec-appendix-systems-record-register catalogs all sixteen records, noting their producing chapters and the specific invariants they bind, while the machine card in @sec-boundary-running-machine specifies the foundational physical parameters of the robot itself.

This four-stage route is a repeatable discipline for making learned behavior dependable in physical space. Four misconceptions, each imported from a field where it holds, routinely distort that work.

## Fallacies and Pitfalls {#sec-boundary-fallacies-pitfalls}

The misconceptions that follow arise when assumptions from pure software engineering, statistical learning, or classical control theory are imported into embodied machines. In digital systems, an erroneous state can typically be trapped, rolled back, or restarted. Across the causal boundary, however, software outputs become physical forces that alter the world irrevocably. Preventing physical harm requires hard deterministic guarantees that learning objectives, human operators, and asynchronous recovery routines cannot provide on their own.

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Fallacy**: *Safety constraints can be trained into the policy.*

Engineering teams often attempt to enforce physical safety by adding penalty terms, barrier penalties, or negative rewards to the training objective. While penalty shaping suppresses undesirable actions over the training distribution, it provides no mathematical guarantee on the actions emitted during deployment. Deep neural networks remain uncalibrated function approximators when exposed to out-of-distribution inputs, sensor degradation, or novel environmental dynamics. A statistical loss function optimizes expected performance, but safety requires hard invariants that hold on every control cycle. For this reason, deterministic safety enforcement must sit downstream of the policy, operating as an independent permission path that filters proposed commands before they reach actuator driver registers, exactly where the third law places the boundary gate.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Pitfall**: *Treating human supervisory intervention as instantaneous in shared-autonomy systems.*

In shared-autonomy designs, such as a robotic surgical tool providing haptic guidance from a learned anatomical model, system designers sometimes treat the human operator as a failsafe catch-all. This assumption ignores the physiological limits of human reaction time, which ranges between 150 ms and 250 ms for simple tactile or visual reflexes and grows under cognitive load. Once console video and a handshake are added, the running machine's card budgets an in-loop takeover at `{python} MachineCard.value_str["t_takeover_in"]`. Over that interval, an actuator running on a 1 kHz control loop can execute hundreds of unchecked cycles, generating enough force to tear soft tissue or damage a mechanical workpiece before the operator can intervene. Delegating authority to a human supervisor does not eliminate the machine's capacity for harm during the supervisory lag. The permission path must enforce local force, velocity, and displacement envelopes autonomously, preserving the established physical envelopes under their operating assumptions without relying on timely human overrides.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Pitfall**: *Assuming software latency merely degrades performance gracefully.*

In purely digital systems, inference latency or scheduler jitter increases response time or degrades service quality. In physical systems, timing is a functional correctness requirement. If a learned policy stalls, whether from accelerator kernel contention, memory allocation pauses, or network serialization delays, allowing its previous command to persist across subsequent control cycles turns stale intent into physical danger. For example, a mobile manipulator that repeats its last forward-velocity command during a 100 ms inference hiccup can collide with an unmapped obstacle. Actuation commands must therefore carry bounded temporal validity, enforced by hardware or real-time software watchdogs. When that validity window (the chunk lease of the stopping budget) expires without a verified update, the low-level controller must begin a fallback within its established response budget. The selected stop or hold must remain feasible for the current mechanism, state, and surviving resources.

:::

::: {.fallacy-pitfall}

**Fallacy**: *Assuming physical actuation is reversible through subsequent software compensation.*

Transactional software architectures rely on rollbacks and compensation routines to undo erroneous operations. In embodied systems, thermodynamics and materials science break this equivalence. If a robotic arm applies excessive torque to a workpiece, issuing a reverse motor command cannot unbend plastically deformed metal, repair fractured composite, or recover the electrical energy dissipated as heat in the motor windings ($\MotorPhaseRmsCurrent^2 \PhaseResistance$). Anomaly detection routines that react after physical contact can only truncate ongoing damage; they cannot undo the mechanical work already transferred across the causal boundary. Preventive verification, such as checking proposed trajectories against workspace boundaries, torque limits, and kinetic energy caps before dispatch, must serve as the primary defense. Reactive recovery strategies remain necessary for unexpected disturbances, but they function as a secondary backstop rather than a substitute for preventive enforcement.

:::

## Summary {#sec-boundary-summary}

Physical AI converges two historically distinct engineering disciplines: classical robotics and modern machine learning. As learned models move progressively closer to direct actuator control, the boundary between digital computation and physical reality sharpens at the causal boundary, the interface where an admitted command becomes an irreversible physical effect. In purely software systems, state rollbacks and retries can recover from algorithmic faults; in the physical world, software cannot undo kinetic energy, momentum, or impact. Safe recovery requires an executable, physically feasible countermeasure.

Physical dynamics also do not pause while neural networks compute. Because a machine continues to travel during sensing and processing delays, safety requires deterministic admission checks upstream of any consequential actuation. As the warehouse mobile manipulator's stopping budget and the Tempe collision show, prediction quality offers no protection once response delay has spent the clearance. The architecture resolves this tension by separating proposal from permission and giving an independent, bounded-latency permission path the authority to refuse. Four laws, one physical and three design principles, organize the framework the rest of the book develops.

The chapter's quantitative core is the elementary stopping budget and its crossover speed (@tbl-01-key-equations).

| Equation                                                                                                                              | What it bounds or decides                                                                                                                                                   | Derived                                                             |
|:--------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------|:--------------------------------------------------------------------|
| $\StoppingDistance = \SpeedAtDetection\PrebrakeDelay + \dfrac{\SpeedAtDetection^2}{2\CredibleBrakingDeceleration} \le \ClearDistance$ | Whether a moving machine can stop within its observed clearance: distance traveled during response delay plus braking distance, prior to allowances added in later chapters | @eq-boundary-stopping-budget                                        |
| $\StoppingCrossoverSpeed = 2\CredibleBrakingDeceleration\PrebrakeDelay$                                                               | The crossover speed at which delay distance equals braking distance; below $\StoppingCrossoverSpeed$, delay travel is larger, while above it, braking travel is larger      | From @eq-boundary-stopping-budget, @sec-boundary-kinematic-roofline |

: **Key equations of the causal boundary**: The elementary stopping budget and its crossover speed, with the place each is derived. {#tbl-01-key-equations tbl-colwidths="[34,46,20]"}

::: {.callout-takeaways title="Engineering across the causal boundary"}
* **Useful behavior requires an integrated machine**: Physical AI combines learned decision-making, physical dynamics, and delegated mechanical authority. Delivering reliable autonomous operation requires co-designing task competence with physical body limits, real-time compute runtimes, and the operational evidence supporting deployment.
* **Response delay consumes physical margin**: The elementary stopping budget $\StoppingDistance = \SpeedAtDetection\PrebrakeDelay + \SpeedAtDetection^2/(2\CredibleBrakingDeceleration) \le \ClearDistance$ partitions stopping distance into latency-induced travel and mechanical braking. Below the crossover speed $\StoppingCrossoverSpeed = 2\CredibleBrakingDeceleration\PrebrakeDelay$, response delay dominates stopping distance; above $\StoppingCrossoverSpeed$, braking deceleration dominates. For the warehouse mobile manipulator at its drive limit, pre-braking travel adds `{python} StoppingBudget.blind_share_str` to braking distance. The decisive delay belongs to whichever path triggers the protective response, which can operate independently of the learned proposer's inference time.
* **Proposal and permission serve distinct architectural roles**: The learned proposer (the Brain) generates goal-directed actions, while an independent permission path admits, modifies, or rejects them before they cross the causal boundary. Safety enforcement relies on validated sensor inputs, physical kinematic envelopes, strict real-time deadlines, and verifiable fallback maneuvers.
* **Evidence governs safe operation and systematic refinement**: Four laws structure this book. Irreversibility is a physical law; the other three (endogenous data, proposal is not permission, and permission must be earned) are design principles that translate covariate shift, runtime assurance, and the assurance case into systems practice. Together they link physical hardware, embodied learning, real-time execution, and operational governance, establishing verified service within defined operational envelopes while identifying the targeted evaluations needed to expand them.
:::

Before judging whether a proposed action is right, an engineer should establish what physical response would remain if the proposal were wrong, stale, or never arrived, and whether the machine still holds the clearance, the time, and the authority to carry that response out. A design that cannot answer from its own measured limits has handed safety to prediction quality, and the stopping budget showed that prediction quality cannot buy back clearance once delay has spent it. The answer therefore starts from what the plant can do under stated conditions, never from what the model believes.

## Historical Perspective and Further Reading {#sec-boundary-history}

In physical artificial intelligence, moving learned models directly into the actuation loop creates severe timing and safety hazards. The engineering principles that resolve these challenges originate in embedded systems, real-time control, and safety engineering. General-purpose computing treats execution time as a mere performance optimization, assuming that correctness depends solely on logical input-output relationships. Cyber-physical systems theory overturned this assumption, holding that physical dynamics and computational processes must be modeled jointly because a command dispatched at the wrong time is physically incorrect [@lee2008cyber]. This insight forms the foundation of the causal boundary. Similarly, separating command proposal from execution permission stems from runtime assurance architectures. The Simplex architecture demonstrated that an industrial control system could safely run an unverified, high-performance controller if paired with a certified baseline controller and deterministic switching logic capable of taking back the plant before safety boundaries were violated [@seto1998simplex; @sha2001using]. Modern safety filters in embodied machine learning generalize this design, validating neural network proposals against mathematical certificates of safe states (control barrier functions or reachability envelopes, which @sec-enforcement develops) before granting actuator permission [@hsu2024safetyfilter].

Many foundational safety principles in physical systems emerged from forensic investigations of catastrophic failures. The Therac-25 radiation therapy disasters demonstrated the fatal peril of replacing mechanical interlocks with software routines [@leveson1993investigating]. When race conditions bypassed software checks, the machine administered lethal radiation overdoses, proving that software reliability does not imply system safety. Systems-theoretic safety subsequently recast accidents not as isolated component breakdowns, but as failures of the overall control structure to enforce safety constraints on the interactions among components, feedback loops, and human operators [@leveson2011engineering]. This shift led directly to the assurance case, a structured argument demonstrating that concrete evidence satisfies defined safety claims within explicit operating environments [@kelly1998arguing]. The UL 4600 standard adopted this structure as its central framework for autonomous products [@ul4600], abandoning arbitrary road-testing mileage in favor of verifiable, claim-based arguments. Public accident records, particularly the National Transportation Safety Board investigation of the 2018 Tempe autonomous vehicle collision [@ntsb2019uber], remain the field's most complete documentation of how safety arguments unravel when classification changes, a response delay chosen in software, and reliance on a human fallback interact in the field.

- **Cyber-physical systems** [@lee2008cyber]. Lee articulates why classical computing abstractions fail when computation interacts with physical processes. General-purpose computer architectures deliberately abstract away time, treating execution speed as a performance consideration rather than a correctness specification. Lee demonstrates that for physical interactions, the timing of an actuation command is inseparable from its physical meaning, providing the conceptual foundation for treating the causal boundary as an explicit systems interface.
- **Runtime assurance** [@sha2001using]. Sha's paper on the Simplex architecture is the place to see how the switching logic decides when to take the plant back from the unverified controller, and why that logic must be simpler than what it supervises. It is the pattern behind this book's separation of proposal from permission.
- **Therac-25** [@leveson1993investigating]. Leveson and Turner's forensic analysis traces the specific race conditions and the development and reporting practices that let the overdoses recur, detail the summary above omits. It remains the essential case study in why protective functions need justification independent of the software they supervise.
- **Systems-theoretic safety** [@leveson2011engineering]. Leveson introduces the STAMP accident model, reframing safety as a continuous control problem rather than a collection of component failure probabilities. Accidents occur when the control structure fails to enforce safety constraints across component interactions, sensor delays, and feedback loops. This text provides the theoretical basis for enforcing safety invariants as dynamic runtime constraints rather than static design assumptions.
- **The Tempe investigation** [@ntsb2019uber]. The National Transportation Safety Board report on the fatal 2018 Tempe autonomous vehicle crash offers the most thorough empirical record of an embodied AI safety failure. The report details how classification changes that discarded tracking history, a one-second action suppression meant to limit responses to false alarms, the separate deactivation of the vehicle's factory emergency braking over possible radar interference, and reliance on an operator whose attention nothing monitored combined in the collision. The event timeline and sensor telemetry provide vital reading for anyone building real-time perception-action loops.

::: {.callout-chapter-connection title="From the causal boundary to physical limits"}
A permission decision needs a physical limit against which to judge the proposed action. @Sec-body begins Part I with the five budgets the permission path must check before it commits torque (measurement freshness, stopping distance, deliverable torque, winding heat, and supply voltage) and asks which binds first for a given maneuver, under what stress, and on what evidence. Each budget ends as a limit record, the six-element form this chapter sketched from its stopping calculation. @Sec-brain then examines the learned proposer's capabilities and timing, and @sec-nervous uses both sets of constraints to design the handoff and independent permission path. The progression starts with what the machine can sustain and ends with how computation may safely request it.
:::
